Comment: llmops-pipeline — stage DAG with waitForTaskToken per harness task and the self-iteration remediation loop (eval gate fail -> remediate finetune, <=3 iterations, then escalate). TimeoutSeconds is the ONLY real ceiling on a stage: the driver Lambda's own 900s limit does not bound the stage, because it self-reinvokes across invocations via _continuation, but the task token it holds only lives for TimeoutSeconds. The six states that wait on real work (generate, curate, finetune launch, eval generate, eval gate, remediate) carry 86400 — a full day, on the platform owner's instruction, after a 480-teacher-call generation run was cut off at 7200s mid-work. The seven that do bookkeeping keep their hour: a wedged Teardown at 86400 would leave an ml.g5.2xlarge endpoint InService for a day at $1.515/hr, which is the exact shape of the 843-day orphan this project already paid for. NO harness state carries HeartbeatSeconds, and that is a decision rather than an omission -- a guard test in tests/test_orchestration.py fails if one appears. HeartbeatSeconds is a first-class part of .waitForTaskToken and it looks like the AWS-native replacement for the driver's own liveness beat plus the resurrector, but the two cannot coexist and the native one is the weaker of the pair here. A heartbeat timeout makes Step Functions fail the state itself, mint a NEW random task token on the retry, and it does not terminate the harness that stopped beating (only .sync has best-effort cancellation; the callback pattern promises nothing) -- so the orphan keeps streaming, keeps burning account-level TPM the whole fleet shares, and keeps writing its own liveness beat. The resurrector recovers the SAME session on the SAME token from the parked payload, which keeps the partial work of a stage that is neither cheap nor idempotent (S3 manifest append and a wall-clock DDB sort key are both non-idempotent, which is also why these states carry Retry: NONE). Two independent authorities to declare a stage dead means two independent dispatches of its replacement, so exactly one may hold that authority, and it is the one that resumes rather than restarts.

PipelineModeChoice.Comment: data_audit is the conductor's starter: audit the customer's data and stop -- no GPU stage may run. eval_only re-enters an artifact a PREVIOUS run already paid for and re-judges it: no data-prep, no training, and it stops at the gate verdict without deploying, because re-measuring is not re-approving. It exists because r6c's 8B run produced a 12.2 GiB model and a gate the reformed metric had to re-score, and with only full/data_audit the only way to re-judge was a script in someone's working directory -- unversioned, unaudited, and invisible to the run table. deploy_only enters at Deploy against an artifact params.model_artifact_uri names, and it exists because the last five states of this machine (Deploy, SmokeTest, MonitorHealth, Teardown, MonitorReport) had never executed ONCE: 38 runs, 33 failed, and the single row marked completed carries one data-prep stage event. Their only entry is QualityGateChoice, gate_passed has never been true, so every defect in serving lived behind a door no run could open -- and this platform's dominant failure is exactly that shape, a capability the docs, the prompt and the IAM all describe that nothing can reach (five separate runs died on a missing grant for a call the code always makes). It is a REHEARSAL lane, not a shortcut: it does not soften the gate, it cannot be entered from inside a run, and its existence is not permission to bypass QualityGateChoice -- see EvalOnlyStopChoice, which refuses the far weaker version of the same move. What makes it legitimate is that the dispatch IS the approval, the same way eval_only's is: MODE_REQUIRED_PARAMS forces the operator to name the exact artifact rather than letting an agent pick the newest one in the bucket, and params.model_package_approval_status keeps what smoke registers at PendingManualApproval so a rehearsal can never leave an Approved model package behind. Default full pipeline otherwise.

FinetuneLaunch.Comment: Carried HeartbeatSeconds: 18000 until 2026-08-03, and it was a second, SHORTER deadline rather than the liveness signal it looks like: nothing in this platform ever calls SendTaskHeartbeat (grep the repo -- zero sites; the only reader of the field is the console's hover card, which merely displays it). So the first heartbeat never arrived and this state actually died at 18000s while its TimeoutSeconds said 21600. Removed rather than kept, because a heartbeat interval with no sender is a deadline nobody can see: the number in the ASL was not the number that fired. If a real heartbeat is ever implemented in the driver's continuation loop, this field comes back WITH it, and test_a_heartbeat_interval_requires_something_to_send_heartbeats is what will let it back in.

Catch.Comment: A tracked job stopped with $0 billed (capacity race loser / quota wait) re-enters this state with $.iteration UNCHANGED -- capacity is weather, not a code failure, so it spends no remediation iteration. The loop guard is resume_pipeline's capacity_retries cap: the 4th stop arrives as TrainingJobFailed.

EvalGenerate.Comment: Prepare the eval and either finish synchronously or launch student inference as a SageMaker job via job_launched (launch-and-release, same shape as FinetuneLaunch). Before this was a launch/score pair, the eval agent had no legal way to span a long inference job except polling in-turn -- which is exactly where prose turn-ends happen; run-20260808T024809Z-b56281da died there with a healthy job mid-flight and nobody listening.

Catch.Comment: A tracked job stopped with $0 billed (capacity race loser / quota wait) re-enters this state with $.iteration UNCHANGED -- capacity is weather, not a code failure, so it spends no remediation iteration. The loop guard is resume_pipeline's capacity_retries cap: the 4th stop arrives as TrainingJobFailed.

A FAILED eval inference job is an inference-code defect, not a model defect -- so it re-enters THIS state (the eval agent diagnoses its own failed job and fixes its own code), never RemediateFinetune, which re-trains: found live on run-20260811T040003Z-3548116f, where retraining could not have removed the quotes an SDK-encoded hyperparameter carried into the final put_object.

EvalScore.Comment: Fresh session after the inference job completed (or immediately, if evaluate finished synchronously -- the score task is idempotent when evaluation/report.json already exists). Produces the report EvalGate reads.

EvalOnlyStopChoice.Comment: In eval_only BOTH verdicts end the run at the report. A pass must not reach Deploy: the plan a human signed in this mode bought a measurement of an existing artifact, not an endpoint, and an autonomous deploy off a re-judge is a spend nobody approved. A fail must not reach RemediationChoice either: IncrementIteration leads to RemediateFinetune, which would launch GPU training in a mode whose entry deliberately skipped it -- and there is no finetune stage in this manifest for it to remediate. The gate verdict is in gate.json either way, exactly as data_audit's readiness verdict is in its report.

RemediationChoice.Comment: Self-iteration budget: remediate while iteration < 3, then escalate to human.

IncrementIteration.Comment: Parameters with no ResultPath REPLACES the state document, so this object is the whole state on every remediating run. It must therefore hand back everything start_pipeline seeded into the execution input: task_id is read by MarkTaskDone/MarkTaskFailed at closeout, and a JSONPath that is not present raises States.Runtime, which no Catch can intercept — the run dies mid-flight with the conductor's task row left open. test_a_state_replacing_pass_hands_back_the_whole_entry_contract derives this list from start_pipeline's handler so it cannot rot.

Catch.Comment: This state LAUNCHES a training job (the remediate task applies its one targeted change and relaunches), so it parks a task token that resume_pipeline settles exactly like FinetuneLaunch's -- that Lambda reads the parked token off the run row and never asks which state parked it. Until 2026-08-13 the only Catch here was States.ALL, so a $0-billed capacity stop on a remediation relaunch went to EscalateFail: the cheapest possible non-failure killed the run at the one moment it was already recovering. Same shape as FinetuneLaunch's: re-enter with $.iteration UNCHANGED, because capacity is weather, and let resume_pipeline's capacity_retries cap be the loop guard.

A remediation whose own job fails is a spent iteration, not an escalation: RemediationChoice re-checks the iteration budget and only escalates once it is exhausted. Terminates because IncrementIteration is on the path back here.

Still lands on the teardown path, now via MonitorHealth, whose own Catch goes straight to Teardown. A failed smoke test is exactly when the endpoint's metrics are worth reading, and the endpoint is still alive here.

MonitorHealth.Comment: MonitorHealth had no state at all until now, and llmops_monitor's three declared tasks (health, sweep, report) had ZERO dispatch sites anywhere in the platform -- the same defect class as an emitted event with no rule: a capability the docs, the prompt and the IAM all describe, that nothing can ever reach. Placement is forced by the shape of the work, not by taste: `health` reads CloudWatch metrics for a LIVE endpoint, and Teardown ALWAYS deletes that endpoint (its own Comment says so, including on SmokeTest's Catch). So between SmokeTest and Teardown is the only window in a run's life where the thing being monitored exists. After Teardown the endpoint is gone and get-metric-data returns an empty series that reads identically to a healthy idle endpoint.

Catch.Comment: Health is observation, not a gate: a CloudWatch read that fails must never strand the endpoint it was watching. Routes to Teardown for the same reason SmokeTest's Catch does -- an orphaned endpoint is the #1 cost risk, and it costs money whether or not we managed to measure it.

Teardown.Comment: Always runs after deploy — orphaned endpoints are the #1 cost risk.

MonitorReport.Comment: The run's story, consolidated once the manifest is finished. Placed AFTER Teardown rather than before it because the report enumerates the stage timeline and total estimated cost from the manifest -- run before Teardown it would publish a report whose last line is missing, and teardown is precisely the entry a cost reader looks for. It is the last harness task in the run, so it cannot be a gate either.

Catch.Comment: A report that failed to write must not fail a run whose pipeline succeeded. The narrative is a deliverable; the run's terminal state is a fact. Complete still emits PipelineCompleted and MarkRunDone still closes the record.

Complete.Comment: ResultPath keeps $.run_id and $.task_id in the state for MarkTaskDone. Same trap EscalateFail fell into: without it the PutEvents response becomes the whole state and the next state dies on a missing path.

MarkRunDone.Comment: The success-path twin of MarkRunFailed, and the asymmetry it closes was live for as long as the failure path was fixed: runs.status was only ever written 'running' (start_pipeline), 'escalated' (the driver) or 'failed' (MarkRunFailed). NOTHING wrote 'completed'. stage_complete updates the manifest and settles the task token; it never touches the run's own status. So a run that succeeded stayed at status=running forever while its execution read SUCCEEDED -- the same zombie MarkRunFailed exists to prevent, on the happy path. It went unseen because until run-20260801T062313Z-4d3e2e69 no execution had ever SUCCEEDED; the fix for the failure path could not have revealed it. Observed 2026-08-01: that run's task row closed correctly at 06:34:43Z while its run row still read 'running' five hours later. ConditionExpression mirrors MarkRunFailed's so a richer terminal status already written by the driver (escalated) is kept rather than overwritten, and Catch: States.ALL means a rejected condition or a DDB outage cannot fail an execution whose pipeline genuinely succeeded.

Catch.Comment: Both exits go to MarkTaskDone for the same reason MarkRunFailed's Catch goes to MarkTaskFailed: the run record and the task record are separate records with separate reasons to go stale, so failing to close one must not leave the other open.

MarkTaskDone.Comment: Close out the conductor's task record on the SUCCESS path. A run dispatched from an approved plan has two records with lifecycles -- the run and the llmops-tasks row -- and only the run was ever closed, so the console's Tasks tab showed a finished order as still in flight and the audit trail never recorded how it ended. llmops-tasks is written only by the console Lambda, which is not in the execution path, so the state machine does it, as it already does for the run record. The ConditionExpression makes the NO_TASK sentinel a no-op: most runs (schedule, webhook) have no task, and attempting the write anyway would either mint a phantom task row or fail a healthy execution.

Catch.Comment: No task (sentinel), or a task already in a richer terminal state. Neither is a run failure -- the run genuinely succeeded, so swallow and end.

EscalateFail.Comment: ResultPath files the PutEvents response under a key instead of letting it become the whole state. Without it, a Task's result REPLACES its input -- and the next state, MarkRunFailed, reads $.run_id, which a PutEvents response does not contain. The zombie-closeout fix would have failed on a missing path at the exact moment it was needed, leaving the run at status=running: the bug it was written to fix.

Detail.reason: Terminal failure or remediation budget exhausted -- see the stage events for the failing stage.

Fail.Cause: Terminal failure or remediation budget exhausted — see EscalatedToHuman event, SNS, and DDB stage events.

MarkRunFailed.Comment: Close out the run record. Every Python writer of runs.status lives inside a stage Lambda, so a stage that CRASHES leaves the run at status=running forever while its execution is FAILED -- a zombie the console shows as live. The state machine is the only participant still alive when a stage dies, so it writes the terminal status itself, through the SDK integration rather than yet another Lambda. A rejected condition means the driver already wrote a RICHER terminal status (escalated) -- the Catch keeps it and carries on to Fail. Catching States.ALL also means a DDB outage cannot hang the execution: the run still ends FAILED, just without the marker.

MarkTaskFailed.Comment: The failure-path twin of MarkTaskDone. Both of MarkRunFailed's exits route here, including its Catch: a DDB error while closing the RUN must not stop us from closing the TASK, since those are separate records and separate reasons to be stale. Observed live: task-58ecde82adcd73bf sat at 'dispatched' for a day after run-20260731T183103Z-8b864805 read 'failed', because nothing on this path wrote the task at all. Ends at Fail either way, so the execution still reports FAILED.

Catch.Comment: No task (sentinel) or already terminal -- the run still failed, so go to Fail regardless.

RemediationChoiceEval.Comment: Same self-iteration budget as RemediationChoice, but the eval loop re-enters EvalGenerate: the failure being remediated lives in the eval agent's own inference code, and the finetune loop's RemediateFinetune would spend GPU money re-training a model that is not the problem.

IncrementIterationEval.Comment: State-replacing Pass, same contract obligations as IncrementIteration (the handback guard derives over every such Pass, so this one is under it from birth).
